To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) we can use the click data to predict document relevance, (ii) the predictions are accurate enough to be used to compare ranking functions, and (iii) the predictions can be used with the DCG metric to provide a confidence score for the comparison of ranking algorithms.

(1) we can use a small number of relevance judgments paired to click data to predict relevance for documents that have not yet been judged, and (2) this can be used to improve the accuracy of evaluation metrics for search engines.

we can: (a) use click data to predict relevance, (b) evaluate the performance of ranking functions when only click data is available, and (c) select documents for additional relevance judgments that improve confidence in the ranking.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of evaluating search engines when no relevance judgments are readily available.
the problem of how to evaluate search engines when only a limited number of relevance judgments are available.
the problem of evaluating search engines using clicks, when relevance judgments are unavailable, and with the problem of predicting the relevance of a document when only clicks are available.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our method provides a new way to evaluate ranking functions, and that this evaluation can be done without relevance judgments, and with only a few relevance judgments, when available.

we propose a model that can be used to predict the relevance of a search result based on click data, which can then be used to compare search engines when complete relevance judgments are unavailable.
we have proposed a novel model that allows the comparison of two ranking functions when clicks but not relevance judgments are available.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we provide a novel method to evaluate search engines when relevance judgments are not available, and to identify the better of the ranking functions up to 94%.

we have a method to predict the relevance score for a document given a query and the click data for that query, and this method can be used to compare ranking algorithms when no relevance judgments are present, and to identify the better of the two ranking algorithms when only a few relevance judgments are available.
we propose a novel model to evaluate search engine results when relevance judgments are unavailable, which is the case for the majority of the time in practice.
The main takeaway from our work is that
click data can be used in place of expensive relevance judgments, allowing for the comparison of ranking algorithms across time and across search engines.
click data can be used to improve the evaluation of ranking functions, and that our method is more effective and efficient than previous methods.
click data can be used to predict relevance, and that this can be used to compare ranking functions and to evaluate search engines when complete relevance judgments are unavailable.
